question:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
A great / culture of hospitality of / the Spanish / is well-known.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. A great.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence talks about a specific, well-known culture — "the culture of hospitality of the Spanish" — which is a particular, identifiable culture, not just any random culture.

• Rule — Use of Articles: The definite article "the" is used before a noun that refers to a specific person, place, or thing already known/identified, either by context or by a following phrase (e.g., "of the Spanish"). The indefinite article "a/an" is used only for a non-specific, unidentified singular noun.

• Since the phrase "of hospitality of the Spanish" immediately specifies which culture is being referred to, the noun "culture" must be preceded by "the", not "a".
◦ Correct: The great culture of hospitality of the Spanish is well-known.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "the Spanish" is correct as printed — "the Spanish" correctly uses "the" before a nationality noun used to mean "the Spanish people".

• Option 2: "culture of hospitality of" is grammatically correct in structure; the noun phrase itself is fine.

• Option 4: "is well-known." is correct — the singular subject "the great culture..." correctly takes the singular verb "is".

NOTE

• The definite article "the" is compulsorily used before a noun made specific by a following phrase or clause (e.g., "the book on the table", "the boy who cried wolf").

• Commonly tested article errors in SSC exams: missing "the" before superlatives, before unique objects (the sun, the moon), and before nouns specified by "of" phrases.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
After a while, / she look up / and saw that / it was getting dark.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. she look up.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes actions that already happened, as shown by the past tense verbs "saw" and "was getting".

• Rule — Tense Consistency: All the main verbs in a sentence describing a single sequence of past events must remain in the same tense (Simple Past) unless there is a valid reason to shift.

• The verb "look" in the segment "she look up" is in the base form (V1), which is incorrect here; it must be changed to the past form "looked" (V2) to match the rest of the sentence.
◦ Correct: After a while, she looked up and saw that it was getting dark.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "and saw that" is correct — "saw" is the correct Simple Past form of "see".

• Option 2: "it was getting dark" is correct — "was getting" is the correct Past Continuous form describing an ongoing background action.

• Option 4: "After a while" is a correct time adverbial phrase and needs no change.

NOTE

• A frequent SSC error-spotting trap is a base-form verb (V1) appearing where a past-form verb (V2) is required because the rest of the sentence is clearly in the past tense.

• Other easily confused irregular verb pairs: see–saw–seen, look–looked–looked, go–went–gone, take–took–taken.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
There was an gang of thieves spotted at our local bank, make sure to be careful.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. There was an gang.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The noun "gang" begins with the consonant sound /g/.

• Rule — Use of "a" and "an": The article "a" is used before words beginning with a consonant sound, while "an" is used before words beginning with a vowel sound.

• Since "gang" starts with a consonant sound, it must be preceded by "a", not "an".
◦ Correct: There was a gang of thieves spotted at our local bank, make sure to be careful.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "at our local bank" is grammatically correct and needs no change.

• Option 2: "make sure to be careful" is correct in form.

• Option 4: "of thieves spotted" is correct as printed.

NOTE

• The choice between "a" and "an" depends on the sound, not the letter — e.g., "an hour" (silent h), "a university" (sounds like "yoo").

• Other commonly tested cases: a European, an heir, a one-way street, an MBA.

question:
Select the option that will improve the given sentence by using the most appropriate verb.
Alexa have being working as a teacher for five years now.
option_1: Alexa has been working as a teacher for five years now.
option_2: Alexa has working as a teacher for five years now.
option_3: Alexa is being working as a teacher for five years now.
option_4: Alexa was been working as a teacher for five years now.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Alexa has been working as a teacher for five years now.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes an action that started in the past and is still continuing in the present, with a duration given ("for five years").

• Rule — Present Perfect Continuous Tense:
◦ Structure: Subject + has/have + been + V1+ing + since/for + Object
◦ Has is used with third person singular subjects (he/she/it/Alexa); have is used with I/we/you/they.

• Since the subject "Alexa" is third person singular, the correct auxiliary is "has", and the correct participle form is "been working", not "have being working".
◦ Correct: Alexa has been working as a teacher for five years now.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "has working" omits the auxiliary "been", which is compulsory in the Present Perfect Continuous.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "is being working" is not a valid tense form; a gerund cannot follow "being" in this way.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "was been working" wrongly combines Past tense "was" with "been", which is grammatically invalid.

NOTE

• Time expressions like "for five years", "since 2019", "for a long time" are strong indicators of the Present Perfect / Present Perfect Continuous tense.

• Common auxiliary verb errors tested by SSC: has/have confusion, missing "been" in perfect continuous forms, and wrong combination of two auxiliaries (e.g., "was been", "is being working").

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

How does a camel survive in the desert? Many people think that the camel stores water in its hump, but the hump is really made up of fats. When a camel (1)______ find water, it passes less urine to conserve (2)______ small amount of water it has in its body. Furthermore, the camel has a higher body temperature than (3)______ of most mammals. This means that it starts to sweat (4)________ a higher temperature than that which human beings, for example, (5)________ to perspire. This also helps it to keep water loss through sweating to a minimal.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. cannot.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes what happens "When a camel _____ find water" — logically, the camel conserves water only when it is unable to find any.

• Rule — Modal Verbs of Ability/Inability: "Cannot" (can + not) expresses inability to do something, and is used with a base-form verb (find).

• The sense required here is inability — a camel that cannot find water starts conserving the little water it has, which logically connects to the rest of the sentence about "passing less urine to conserve" water.
◦ Correct: When a camel cannot find water, it passes less urine to conserve...

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "do not" is incorrect because it does not agree with the singular subject "a camel" (should be "does not"), and does not clearly express genuine inability.

• Option 3: "hasn't" is incorrect because "hasn't" must be followed by a past participle (e.g., "hasn't found"), not the base form "find".

• Option 4: "can" is incorrect because it reverses the intended meaning — "can find" would mean the camel is able to find water, which contradicts the logic of water conservation described next.

NOTE

• Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, must, should, will, would) are always followed by the base form (V1) of the verb, never "to + verb" or a participle.

• Subject-verb agreement errors with "do/does" and "has/have" before a base verb are a frequently tested SSC error type.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

How does a camel survive in the desert? Many people think that the camel stores water in its hump, but the hump is really made up of fats. When a camel (1)______ find water, it passes less urine to conserve (2)______ small amount of water it has in its body. Furthermore, the camel has a higher body temperature than (3)______ of most mammals. This means that it starts to sweat (4)________ a higher temperature than that which human beings, for example, (5)________ to perspire. This also helps it to keep water loss through sweating to a minimal.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. the.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "____ small amount of water it has in its body" refers to a specific, particular quantity of water — the exact amount the camel's own body contains — not any random amount.

• Rule — Use of "the": The definite article "the" is used before a noun that is made specific by a following qualifying phrase or clause (here, "...of water it has in its body").

• Since the relative clause "it has in its body" specifies exactly which amount of water is meant, "the" is the correct choice.
◦ Correct: ...it passes less urine to conserve the small amount of water it has in its body.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "which" is incorrect because a relative pronoun cannot be used here — the blank must be an article/determiner before the noun phrase "small amount", not a connector.

• Option 3: "a" is incorrect because the indefinite article "a" would suggest any unspecified small amount, which contradicts the fact that a specific amount (the water already in its body) is being referred to.

• Option 4: "very" is incorrect because "very" is an intensifying adverb used before adjectives, and cannot function as a determiner before the noun phrase "small amount".

NOTE

• A noun followed by a defining relative clause (with or without "that/which/who") almost always takes "the", since the clause makes the noun specific.

• Do not confuse determiners (a, an, the, this, that) with relative pronouns (which, that, who) — they serve different grammatical functions.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

How does a camel survive in the desert? Many people think that the camel stores water in its hump, but the hump is really made up of fats. When a camel (1)______ find water, it passes less urine to conserve (2)______ small amount of water it has in its body. Furthermore, the camel has a higher body temperature than (3)______ of most mammals. This means that it starts to sweat (4)________ a higher temperature than that which human beings, for example, (5)________ to perspire. This also helps it to keep water loss through sweating to a minimal.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. that.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence compares the camel's body temperature with the body temperature "of most mammals" — to avoid repeating the noun "temperature", a pronoun substitute is needed.

• Rule — Use of "that/those" as a Substitute Pronoun: "That" is used to replace a singular, previously mentioned noun in a comparison, to avoid repetition (e.g., "The climate of India is hotter than that of England").

• Here, "that" stands in for "body temperature" (singular), making the comparison grammatically complete and non-repetitive.
◦ Correct: ...has a higher body temperature than that of most mammals.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "some" is incorrect because it does not logically or grammatically complete the comparison "higher... than ___ of most mammals"; it leaves the comparison without a clear referent noun.

• Option 2: "the" is incorrect because an article alone cannot substitute for the noun "temperature" in a comparison — "than the of most mammals" is ungrammatical.

• Option 4: "all" is incorrect for the same reason as "some" — it does not stand in for the noun "temperature" and produces an incomplete comparison.

NOTE

• In comparisons, "that" substitutes a singular noun and "those" substitutes a plural noun, e.g., "The rules of this game are stricter than those of chess."

• This is a very frequently tested cloze-passage pattern in SSC exams: comparative structures using "that of" / "those of".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

How does a camel survive in the desert? Many people think that the camel stores water in its hump, but the hump is really made up of fats. When a camel (1)______ find water, it passes less urine to conserve (2)______ small amount of water it has in its body. Furthermore, the camel has a higher body temperature than (3)______ of most mammals. This means that it starts to sweat (4)________ a higher temperature than that which human beings, for example, (5)________ to perspire. This also helps it to keep water loss through sweating to a minimal.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. at.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a preposition that connects the verb "sweat" with a specific temperature point — the camel begins sweating once its body reaches a certain temperature level.

• Rule — Preposition "at" with a Point/Level: The preposition "at" is used to indicate a specific point, level, value, or degree (e.g., "at 100 degrees", "at a certain age", "at a higher temperature").

• Since the sentence refers to a specific temperature level at which sweating begins, "at" is the correct preposition.
◦ Correct: it starts to sweat at a higher temperature than that which human beings...

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in" is incorrect because "in" indicates enclosure or a time period/duration, not a specific temperature point.

• Option 2: "with" is incorrect because "with" indicates accompaniment or means, which does not fit the sense of a specific temperature level.

• Option 4: "for" is incorrect because "for" indicates purpose or duration, not a specific point/level.

NOTE

• The preposition "at" is used for exact points: at 5 o'clock, at the age of 10, at the top, at a temperature of.

• Distinguish this from "in" (used for enclosed spaces/larger time periods, e.g., "in July", "in the room") and "on" (used for surfaces/specific days, e.g., "on Monday").

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

How does a camel survive in the desert? Many people think that the camel stores water in its hump, but the hump is really made up of fats. When a camel (1)______ find water, it passes less urine to conserve (2)______ small amount of water it has in its body. Furthermore, the camel has a higher body temperature than (3)______ of most mammals. This means that it starts to sweat (4)________ a higher temperature than that which human beings, for example, (5)________ to perspire. This also helps it to keep water loss through sweating to a minimal.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. start.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the blank verb is "human beings", which is a plural noun.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: A plural subject always takes the base form of the verb (V1) in the Simple Present Tense, without the "-s/-es" ending; only a singular (third person) subject takes the "-s/-es" form.

• Since "human beings" is plural, the correct verb form is "start", not "starts".
◦ Correct: ...than that which human beings, for example, start to perspire.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "started" is incorrect because it is a Past tense form, but the rest of the passage is in the Simple Present Tense.

• Option 3: "starting" is incorrect because the "-ing" form cannot function as the main finite verb of the clause without an auxiliary (is/are starting).

• Option 4: "starts" is incorrect because the "-s" form is used only with singular (third person) subjects like "he/she/it", not with the plural subject "human beings".

NOTE

• Collective/plural expressions such as "human beings", "people", "children", "the police" always take a plural verb form.

• This is one of the most frequently tested SSC error types: singular/plural verb-form mismatch (e.g., "he go" vs "he goes", "they goes" vs "they go").

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Shantanu always buries his head in the sand whenever he explains his professional failures to his father.
option_2: shows a blind eye against social issues
option_4: blames the others for his mistakes
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. hides from the truth.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to bury one's head in the sand" means to refuse to acknowledge or face an unpleasant reality, ignoring a problem by pretending it does not exist. (सच्चाई से मुंह छिपाना / अनदेखा करना)
◦ Example: Instead of addressing the company's falling sales, the manager simply buried his head in the sand.

• The expression comes from the popular (though inaccurate) belief that an ostrich buries its head in the sand to avoid danger, when in fact it is merely resting or tending its eggs.

• In the given sentence, Shantanu avoids confronting the truth about his professional failures when explaining them to his father, which matches the meaning "hides from the truth".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: To turn a blind eye (जानबूझकर अनदेखा करना): To deliberately ignore a fact or wrongdoing one is already aware of — close, but this specifically implies ignoring an external wrongdoing, not denying one's own reality.
◦ Example: The guard turned a blind eye to the workers sneaking out early.

• Option 3: To escape from all the difficulties (सभी कठिनाइयों से बच निकलना): Means to get away from problems altogether, which is broader than the specific idea of denying/ignoring an unpleasant truth.

• Option 4: To blame others for his mistakes (अपनी गलतियों का दोष दूसरों पर डालना): Means shifting responsibility onto someone else, which is a different idea from simply refusing to acknowledge the truth.

NOTE

• Other idioms related to avoidance/denial often asked in SSC: "turn a blind eye" (deliberately ignore), "sweep under the carpet" (hide a problem), and "in denial" (refusing to accept a fact).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The cat's entry into the store room was ___________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. quiet.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a word describing how the cat entered the room — the sentence needs an adjective meaning "making little or no noise; silent".

• The correct word is "quiet", which means calm, silent, or making no noise — exactly fitting the description of a cat's soundless entry.
◦ Correct: The cat's entry into the store room was quiet.

• These four options are commonly confused because of their similar spellings, but they have entirely different meanings and parts of speech.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "quite" means "completely" or "to a certain extent" (an adverb of degree), e.g., "She is quite tall" — it does not describe silence.

• Option 3: "cute" means "attractive or endearing in appearance" — it does not relate to sound or manner of entry.

• Option 4: "quit" is a verb meaning "to stop or leave", which does not fit grammatically as a description after "was".

NOTE

• Commonly confused spelling-lookalike words frequently tested by SSC: quite/quiet, than/then, affect/effect, accept/except, principal/principle.

• Memory tip: "quiet" has an extra "e", giving it one more letter than "quite" — the extra "e" can be linked to the idea of extra silence/peace.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The ________ of the whale is 2 tonnes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. weight.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a noun that can be measured in "tonnes" — a unit used to measure mass/heaviness.

• The correct word is "weight", meaning the heaviness of an object, measured in units such as kilograms or tonnes.
◦ Correct: The weight of the whale is 2 tonnes.

• The other three options are near-homophones/lookalikes of "weight" but carry completely unrelated meanings.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "wait" means "to stay in expectation of something" (a verb), which does not fit as a noun measured in tonnes.

• Option 3: "vet" means a "veterinary doctor" (or informally, to screen/examine something) — irrelevant to measurement in tonnes.

• Option 4: "wet" is an adjective meaning "covered/soaked with liquid" and cannot be measured in tonnes.

NOTE

• Commonly confused homophone/near-homophone pairs tested by SSC: weight/wait, whether/weather, hear/here, break/brake, mail/male.

• "Weight" is always a noun in such contexts and is typically measured in kilograms, grams, tonnes, or pounds.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Grasslands should not be foraged and some places are to be closed for grazing.
option_1: over-grazed and some areas should be
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. over-grazed and some areas should be.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence discusses grasslands being closed "for grazing", so the earlier part should logically talk about excessive grazing — "forage" (searching for food) is not the correct sense here; the intended idea is over-grazing damaging the land.

• Rule — Sentence Improvement (Logical Word Choice + Subject-Verb Agreement): The replacement must (i) use a word that logically fits the context of grazing/grassland management, and (ii) maintain correct subject-verb agreement with the plural subject.

• "Over-grazed" correctly conveys the idea of excessive grazing damaging the grassland, and "some areas should be" correctly uses the modal "should" with the plural subject "areas", continuing logically into "closed for grazing".
◦ Correct: Grasslands should not be over-grazed and some areas should be closed for grazing.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "cut and few areas" is incorrect because "cut" does not convey the idea of excessive grazing, and it lacks a proper auxiliary verb for "few areas ___ closed".

• Option 3: "grazed and some places is" is incorrect because the plural subject "some places" requires the plural verb "are", not the singular "is" — a subject-verb agreement error.

• Option 4: "planted or" is incorrect because "planted" is unrelated to the context of grazing/overuse, and the connector "or" breaks the logical sense before "closed for grazing".

NOTE

• In Sentence Improvement questions, always check both logical/contextual word choice and grammatical accuracy (agreement, tense, articles) — the correct option must satisfy both.

• Commonly confused word pairs in agriculture/ecology contexts: graze/forage, cultivate/plant, harvest/reap.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Things that do not come from the ground not safe to compost.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. are not safe.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the sentence is "Things", which is a plural noun, and the sentence as printed is missing a proper linking verb before "not safe".

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement with "Be" Verbs: A plural subject must be followed by the plural form of the verb "to be", i.e., "are", in the Simple Present Tense.

• The sentence needs the linking verb "are" before "not safe" to be grammatically complete and to correctly agree with the plural subject "Things".
◦ Correct: Things that do not come from the ground are not safe to compost.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "has not been safe" is incorrect because "has" is a singular auxiliary, which does not agree with the plural subject "Things", and it unnecessarily shifts the sense to Present Perfect.

• Option 3: "is not safe" is incorrect because "is" is the singular form of "be" and cannot be used with the plural subject "Things".

• Option 4: "be not safe" is incorrect because the base form "be" cannot function as a finite main verb in a Simple Present statement without an auxiliary like "will" or "should".

NOTE

• Plural subjects (things, people, students, they) always take "are/were"; singular subjects (it, he, she, a thing) take "is/was".

• Watch for sentences where the auxiliary "to be" verb is missing entirely — a common SSC error-spotting/improvement pattern.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the given sentence.
He got medals time after time by following the instructions of his mentor.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Repeatedly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "time after time" means again and again; repeatedly; on many occasions. (बार-बार)
◦ Example: She has proved her talent time after time, winning award after award.

• The phrase emphasises a recurring pattern over a period, not a single or occasional occurrence.

• In the given sentence, he wins medals on multiple occasions by following his mentor's instructions, which matches the meaning "Repeatedly".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Twice (दो बार): Means only two occasions, whereas the idiom implies many repeated occasions, not just two.

• Option 3: Rarely (शायद ही कभी): Means seldom or hardly ever — the exact opposite of the idiom's meaning.

• Option 4: Once (एक बार): Means a single occasion, which contradicts the repeated sense conveyed by "time after time".

NOTE

• Other idioms/phrases expressing repetition often asked in SSC: "again and again", "over and over", "day in and day out", "time and again".

• Do not confuse "time after time" (repeatedly) with "in the nick of time" (just in time) or "against time" (in a hurry to meet a deadline).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
I quietly went out at the door into the veranda.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. through.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes movement from inside a space to outside it, passing via an opening (the door), and ending up in another place (the veranda).

• Rule — Preposition "through": "Through" is used to indicate movement from one side of something to the other, passing within or via it — such as passing through a door, window, or tunnel.

• Since the person moves via the door to reach the veranda, "through" is the correct preposition, not "at", which merely indicates a fixed point/position.
◦ Correct: I quietly went out through the door into the veranda.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No substitution required" is incorrect because "at" indicates a static point/position and does not correctly express passing through an opening while moving.

• Option 2: "by" is incorrect because "by" indicates nearness or the agent/means of an action, not movement through an opening.

• Option 4: "from" is incorrect because "from" indicates a starting point of origin, not the passage/route taken to exit.

NOTE

• Prepositions of movement often tested by SSC: "through" (passing via/within), "across" (from one side to the other on a surface), "along" (movement following a line), "past" (movement beyond a point).

• "At" is a preposition of a fixed point (e.g., "at the door", "at the gate") and should not be used to express movement/passage.

question:
Select the option with the correct spelling to replace the underlined word in the given sentence.
A natural clamity causing huge destruction and loss of life and property.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. calamity.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "calamity" — a serious, unforeseen event causing great damage, loss of life, or distress.
◦ Example: The earthquake was a calamity that devastated the entire region.

• Spelling key: CA + LAM + I + TY. Note the sequence "cal" at the start (not "cla"), followed by "am", and the ending "-ity" (not "-itey"). The word comes from the Latin calamitas, meaning "damage, disaster".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "clamanity" — incorrect; the letters "c" and "l" have been wrongly reordered at the start, and the middle syllable is distorted.

• Option 3: "calamitey" — incorrect; the ending should be "-ity", not "-itey".

• Option 4: "climanity" — incorrect; the first vowel should be "a" (cal-), not "i" (clim-), and the middle syllable is altered.

NOTE

• The related adjective is calamitous, meaning disastrous.

• Other commonly confused "-ity" ending spellings tested by SSC: community, opportunity, majority, curiosity, generosity.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
We should not run after transient pleasures of the world.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Permanent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "transient" means lasting only for a short time; temporary; fleeting. (क्षणिक / अस्थायी)
◦ Example: Fame in showbiz can often be transient, fading away within a few years.

• The antonym of "transient" must convey the opposite idea — something that lasts indefinitely or does not change.

• "Permanent" means lasting or intended to last indefinitely; enduring, which is the direct opposite of "transient". (स्थायी)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Unnatural (अस्वाभाविक): Means not natural or artificial — unrelated to duration, so it is not an antonym of "transient".

• Option 2: Sinful (पापपूर्ण): Means wicked or immoral — a meaning unrelated to permanence/duration.

• Option 4: Joyful (आनंदित): Means full of happiness — an emotional quality, not related to how long something lasts.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "transient": temporary, fleeting, momentary, ephemeral, short-lived.

• Other commonly tested antonym pairs in SSC vocabulary: transient × permanent, ephemeral × eternal, volatile × stable.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Luminous
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Radiant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "luminous" means giving off light; bright or shining, especially in the dark. (प्रकाशमान / चमकीला)
◦ Example: The luminous dial of the watch could be read even in complete darkness.

• "Radiant" means sending out light; shining brightly; bright and glowing, which closely matches the meaning of "luminous". (चमकदार)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Laborious (परिश्रमी / कठिन): Means requiring great effort or hard work — unrelated to brightness or light.

• Option 3: Luxurious (विलासितापूर्ण): Means extremely comfortable or elegant, especially involving great expense — unrelated to giving off light.

• Option 4: Amiable (मिलनसार / सौम्य): Means friendly and pleasant in manner — a personality trait, not related to brightness.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "luminous": bright, glowing, shining, incandescent, lustrous.

• Do not confuse "luminous" (giving off light) with "luxurious" (comfortable/lavish) — they are frequently confused due to similar spelling in SSC vocabulary questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
Modest stores and welcoming residents populated the charming tiny town.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. delightful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "charming" means pleasant, attractive, and delightful; having a pleasing quality that appeals to people. (आकर्षक / मनमोहक)
◦ Example: The couple stayed in a charming little cottage by the lake.

• "Delightful" means causing great pleasure or delight; highly pleasing, which closely matches the positive, appealing sense of "charming" in the sentence describing the tiny town. (सुखद / मनभावन)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Unpleasant (अप्रिय): Means not enjoyable or disagreeable — the opposite of "charming".

• Option 3: Hideous (भयानक / बदसूरत): Means extremely ugly or repulsive — again opposite in meaning to "charming".

• Option 4: Nasty (गंदा / अप्रिय): Means highly unpleasant or unkind — also opposite in sense to "charming".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "charming": attractive, delightful, appealing, enchanting, captivating.

• Note that options 2, 3, and 4 are all negative words, making the single positive option ("delightful") clearly identifiable in such synonym questions.

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the given sentence.
King Zheng is known to lead an army of a million armoured soldiers, a thousand chariots and ten thousand horses in his misssion to conquer the neighbouring kingdoms.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Misssion.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word printed in the sentence is "misssion", which contains three "s" letters in a row — this is incorrect.

• The correct spelling is "mission", spelled with only two "s" letters: M-I-S-S-I-O-N, meaning an important assignment or task, especially one involving travel.
◦ Example: The soldiers were sent on a dangerous mission behind enemy lines.

• Spelling key: MIS + SION. There are exactly two "s" letters — one from "mis-" and one starting "-sion" — never three.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Kingdoms" is spelt correctly — K-I-N-G-D-O-M-S.

• Option 3: "Chariots" is spelt correctly — C-H-A-R-I-O-T-S.

• Option 4: "Thousand" is spelt correctly — T-H-O-U-S-A-N-D.

NOTE

• Words ending in "-sion" or "-ssion" are a common SSC spelling trap: mission, passion, session, permission, discussion — count the letters carefully rather than guessing.

• Other commonly misspelt double-letter words tested by SSC: necessary (one c, two s), occurrence (two c, two r), embarrass (two r, two s).

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
In spring the leaves are bright green, whereas they appear ______ in autumn.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. dull.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "bright" means giving out or reflecting much light; vivid and shining in colour. (चमकीला)
◦ Example: The bright green leaves glistened in the morning sun.

• The blank requires the antonym of "bright" to logically contrast the vivid spring leaves with how they appear in autumn.

• "Dull" means not bright or vivid; lacking brightness, colour, or shine, which is the direct opposite of "bright". (फीका / बेरौनक)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Gleaming (चमकता हुआ): Means shining brightly — this is a synonym of "bright", not its antonym.

• Option 2: Luminous (प्रकाशमान): Means giving off light — again a synonym of "bright", not the opposite.

• Option 3: Dazzling (चकाचौंध करने वाला): Means extremely bright, so bright as to blind temporarily — also a synonym, not an antonym, of "bright".

NOTE

• Other antonym pairs of "bright" tested by SSC: bright × dim, bright × faded, bright × drab.

• A common SSC distractor pattern: three options are synonyms of the given word and only one is the true antonym — always check the exact relationship (synonym vs antonym) asked for.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
It is the _____________ to reach Delhi.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. fastest route.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a superlative phrase describing the best way, in terms of time/speed, to reach Delhi.

• "Fastest route" is the standard, idiomatic collocation used in English to describe the path that takes the least time to travel — "fast/fastest" is the natural collocate of "route" when speed of travel is meant.
◦ Correct: It is the fastest route to reach Delhi.

• While "quick/quickest" also relates to speed, the conventional, idiomatic pairing with "route" in this fixed usage is "fastest route" (compare "shortest route"), making it the most appropriate choice among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "lowest route" is incorrect because "lowest" relates to height or quantity, not speed or distance of travel, making it contextually meaningless here.

• Option 2: "strongest route" is incorrect because "strongest" describes strength/intensity, which does not apply to a travel route.

• Option 3: "quickest route" is a close contextual fit for speed but is not the conventionally preferred collocation compared with "fastest route" in this fixed usage.

NOTE

• Common travel-related collocations tested by SSC: fastest route, shortest distance, direct flight, scenic route.

• Always check which adjective conventionally pairs with the given noun (collocation), not just which one is logically plausible.

question:
Identify the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the following sentence.
Harry's behaviour was very blunt during his school days.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Polite.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "blunt", when used to describe a person's behaviour or speech, means very direct in a way that seems rude or tactless; not gentle or diplomatic. (रूखा / कठोरतापूर्वक स्पष्टवादी)
◦ Example: His blunt remarks about her cooking hurt her feelings.

• The antonym must convey the opposite quality — behaviour that is courteous, gentle, and considerate of others' feelings.

• "Polite" means having or showing good manners and consideration for others; courteous, which is the direct opposite of "blunt" behaviour. (विनम्र / सभ्य)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Excited (उत्साहित): Means feeling great enthusiasm or eagerness — an emotional state unrelated to bluntness/politeness.

• Option 3: Dull (नीरस): Means lacking excitement or interest — this describes personality/liveliness, not directness of manner, so it is not the antonym of "blunt" here.

• Option 4: Curious (जिज्ञासु): Means eager to know or learn something — unrelated to how tactfully one speaks or behaves.

NOTE

• "Blunt" has two related senses: (i) not sharp (a blunt knife) and (ii) direct/tactless in speech or manner — context decides which is meant; here it is the second sense.

• Other antonym pairs of "blunt" (manner sense) tested by SSC: blunt × tactful, blunt × diplomatic, blunt × courteous.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Rectify
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Correct.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "rectify" means to put something right; to correct an error or fault. (सुधारना / ठीक करना)
◦ Example: The technician was called in to rectify the fault in the wiring.

• "Correct", when used as a verb, means to make something right by removing errors or faults, which is exactly synonymous with "rectify". (ठीक करना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Connect (जोड़ना): Means to join or link two things together — unrelated to fixing an error.

• Option 2: Consider (विचार करना): Means to think carefully about something — unrelated to correcting a fault.

• Option 4: Count (गिनना): Means to determine the total number of something — unrelated to the meaning of "rectify".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "rectify": correct, amend, fix, remedy, repair.

• Related noun form: rectification (the act of correcting something), commonly seen in phrases like "rectification of errors" in SSC vocabulary/one-word substitution questions.
